entries.title: CC0
entries.summary: CC0 is a public domain dedication from Creative Commons that lets creators give up their copyright as fully as the law allows.
entries.body:
**CC0** (read "C C zero") is a legal tool published by Creative Commons in 2009. With it, a creator waives all of their copyright and related rights in a work, placing it as completely as possible in the [[public-domain|public domain]].[^1]

## How it works

Not every country lets people simply give away their copyright, so CC0 works in layers:

1. **Waiver**: the creator gives up all of their rights in the work, worldwide.
2. **Fallback license**: where a full waiver is not legally possible, CC0 grants everyone a license to use the work for any purpose, with no conditions.

!#O#No attribution needed# !#Y#Commercial use OK# !#L#No share-alike#

Because of this design, a CC0 work can be used without attribution, without sharing changes, and for commercial purposes.

> [!FACT] The "0" in CC0 stands for zero: zero conditions on how a work can be reused.

## What CC0 does not cover

CC0 only covers rights held by the person applying it. It does not affect #O#trademarks or patents##, and it does not grant rights that other people may hold, such as the privacy rights of a person shown in a photograph.

## Uses

CC0 is widely used for scientific data, museum collections, software, and open knowledge projects such as [[opendb|OpenDB]], where removing every barrier to reuse is the goal.

## References

[^1]: Creative Commons, "CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication", https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/

entries.title: DORFic
entries.summary: DORFic is a bright, minimalist subgenre of the Frutiger Aero design aesthetic, named for daylight, orange, red, futurism and graphic.
entries.body:
{{images needed|an image to represent DORFic}}

**DORFic** is a bright, minimalist design subgenre of [[frutiger-aero|Frutiger Aero]], based on graphic design that was common from the mid-2000s to the mid-2010s.[^wiktionary]

## The name

The name is an acronym for **d**aylight, **o**range, **r**ed, **f**uturism and graph**ic**, with "graphic" shortened to "fic".[^wiktionary]

#O#Orange# #R#Red# #Y#Daylight#

::gamber{DORFic at a glance|Daylight, orange, red, futurism and graphic design}

## Style

Like its parent style, DORFic has a clean, corporate and sterile feel. Instead of Frutiger Aero's nature imagery of skies, water and leaves, it leans toward #O#industrialism and the "Abstract Tech" look##, often showing military and factory imagery balanced with sterile scientific equipment.[^wiktionary]

## History

The look took shape in the mid-to-late 2000s, as mobile technology was advancing quickly, and it appeared mostly in video games and corporate design.[^wiktionary] Like Frutiger Aero itself, the name was given years later by people collecting and discussing these visuals online.

[^wiktionary]: "DORFic", Wiktionary, the free dictionary, including its quotations from frutiger-aero.org and skeuoss.net. https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/DORFic

entries.title: Frutiger Aero
entries.summary: Frutiger Aero is a design style from the mid-2000s to early 2010s known for glossy surfaces, glass, bubbles, water and bright nature imagery.
entries.body:
{{unreferenced}}

**Frutiger Aero** is a name for a visual style that was common in technology products, advertising and websites from roughly the mid-2000s to the early 2010s. It mixes glossy, glass-like interface elements with optimistic images of nature and technology.

![Glossy bubbles over a blue sky](media:aero-bubbles)

## Features

#B#Sky blue# #T#Aqua# #G#Grass green# #W#White#

Some Keydown styles inspired by the look: @faaqua-1@Aqua gel@ @fabubble-1@Soap bubble@ @faglass-1@Glass@ %3%TU%Gel halo%## ^^B^Speech bubble^^

* **Gloss and glass**: buttons and panels with bright highlights, reflections and see-through blurred backgrounds.
* **Nature**: blue skies, green fields, water drops, bubbles, fish and leaves.
* **Bright, clean colors**: especially sky blue, aqua, green and white.
* **Skeuomorphism**: interface parts that look like real, shiny physical objects.

> [!FACT] The look was never officially named while it was popular: "Frutiger Aero" was coined by fans years later.

## The name

The name combines **Frutiger**, a family of clean sans-serif typefaces designed by Adrian Frutiger that is often associated with the look, and **Aero**, the glassy interface theme of Windows Vista and Windows 7. The label itself was created years after the style's peak, when people began collecting and discussing these visuals online.

## Subgenres

Fans of the style have named several subgenres. One example is [[dorfic|DORFic]], a brighter, more industrial variation built around daylight, orange and red.

## Legacy

Flat design largely replaced glossy interfaces in the 2010s, but Frutiger Aero later #TU#became popular again as a nostalgic aesthetic##. Apps such as those in Radii Office use its gel buttons and glass panels on purpose.

entries.title: Grassmann number
entries.summary: A Grassmann number is a number built from generators that anticommute, so that swapping two of them flips the sign and every generator squares to zero.
entries.body:
{{unreferenced}}

A **Grassmann number** (also called an **anticommuting number**) is an element of an algebra built from **generators** $\theta_1, \theta_2, \ldots, \theta_n$ that **anticommute**:

$$\theta_i \theta_j = -\theta_j \theta_i$$

Swapping the order of two generators flips the sign. Taking $i = j$ gives $\theta_i^2 = -\theta_i^2$, so

$$\theta_i^2 = 0$$

::amethyst{Grassmann numbers anticommute: swapping two of them flips the sign, so each one squares to zero.}

Every generator squares to zero, even though it is not zero itself. This is very different from ordinary real or [[imaginary-number|imaginary numbers]], and it is exactly what makes Grassmann numbers useful in physics.

They are named after the German mathematician **Hermann Grassmann**, whose 1844 work *Die lineare Ausdehnungslehre* introduced the algebra behind them, known today as the **exterior algebra**.

## Building Grassmann numbers

Because each generator can appear at most once in a product, every Grassmann number is a finite sum. With one generator $\theta$, the most general element is

$$z = a + b\,\theta$$

for ordinary numbers $a$ and $b$. With two generators it is

$$z = a + b\,\theta_1 + c\,\theta_2 + d\,\theta_1\theta_2$$

In general, $n$ generators give $2^n$ independent terms, one for each subset of the generators (compare the power set in [[set-mathematics|set theory]]).

#%G%Even terms commute% #%PR%Odd terms anticommute%

* Terms with an **even** number of generators, like $\theta_1\theta_2$, commute with everything.
* Terms with an **odd** number of generators anticommute with each other.

Functions are simple too: since $\theta^2 = 0$, any power series stops early. For example, $e^{\theta} = 1 + \theta$.

## Calculus with Grassmann numbers

There is a consistent calculus for these numbers, worked out by the mathematician Felix Berezin, and called **Berezin integration**. For a single generator the rules are

$$\int d\theta \; 1 = 0, \qquad \int d\theta \; \theta = 1$$

so integrating behaves like differentiating.

> [!NOTE] For Grassmann numbers, integration and differentiation follow the same rules.

A key result is the Gaussian integral over pairs of Grassmann variables, which (up to sign and ordering conventions) gives a **determinant**, $\det A$, where the same integral over ordinary numbers gives $1/\sqrt{\det A}$.

## Uses in physics

* **Fermions**: particles such as electrons are fermions, and obey the Pauli exclusion principle, so no two can be in the same state. In the path-integral form of [[quantum-mechanics|quantum mechanics]] and quantum field theory, fermion fields are described by Grassmann numbers, and the rule $\theta^2 = 0$ mirrors the exclusion principle.
* **Supersymmetry**: theories that relate bosons and fermions use **superspace**, which adds Grassmann coordinates to ordinary space and time.
* **Mathematics**: the exterior algebra is used to describe areas, volumes and orientation, and appears in differential geometry as differential forms.

entries.title: Imaginary number
entries.summary: An imaginary number is a real number multiplied by the imaginary unit i, the number whose square is −1.
entries.body:
{{unreferenced}}

An **imaginary number** is a real number multiplied by the **imaginary unit** $i$, which is defined by the property

$$i^2 = -1$$

No real number has a negative square, so $i$ is a new kind of number. Numbers such as $3i$, $-\tfrac{1}{2}i$ and $\sqrt{2}\,i$ are imaginary. Adding a real number and an imaginary number gives a **complex number**, written $a + bi$, where $a$ is the **real part** and $b$ is the **imaginary part**. Zero is the only number that is both real and imaginary.

Despite the name, #PR#imaginary numbers are no less "real"## than negative numbers or fractions: they are a precise and very useful part of mathematics, physics and engineering.

## Square roots of negative numbers

With $i$, every negative number has square roots. Because $(2i)^2 = 4i^2 = -4$, the principal square root of $-4$ is $2i$, and in general $\sqrt{-x} = i\sqrt{x}$ for $x > 0$. Every quadratic equation then has solutions: $x^2 + 1 = 0$ is solved by $x = i$ and $x = -i$.

> [!CAUTION] One familiar rule needs care: $\sqrt{a}\sqrt{b} = \sqrt{ab}$ is not true when both numbers are negative.
> For example, $\sqrt{-1}\sqrt{-1} = i \cdot i = -1$, but $\sqrt{(-1)(-1)} = \sqrt{1} = 1$.

## Powers of i

The powers of $i$ repeat in a cycle of four: %7%B%i%## %7%R%−1%## %7%PR%−i%## %7%G%1%##

* $i^1 = i$
* $i^2 = -1$
* $i^3 = -i$
* $i^4 = 1$

so $i^5 = i$ again, and $i^{n}$ depends only on the remainder when $n$ is divided by 4.

## The complex plane

Complex numbers can be drawn as points in a plane, with the real part along the horizontal axis and the imaginary part along the vertical axis. Imaginary numbers lie on the vertical axis. In this picture, **multiplying by $i$ rotates a number a quarter turn (90°) counterclockwise** around zero: $1 \to i \to -1 \to -i \to 1$.

This link between multiplication and rotation is captured by **Euler's formula**,

$$e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$$

which, with $\theta = \pi$, gives the famous identity $e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0$.

> [!FACT] Euler's identity links five of the most important numbers in mathematics: 0, 1, π, e and i.

## History

* In 1545, Gerolamo Cardano met square roots of negative numbers while solving cubic equations, but treated them as useless.
* In 1572, Rafael Bombelli wrote down the rules for calculating with them, showing they could lead to real answers.
* In 1637, René Descartes called such numbers "imaginary", meaning it as an insult; the name stuck.
* Leonhard Euler introduced the symbol $i$ for $\sqrt{-1}$ in 1777.
* Around 1800, Caspar Wessel and Jean-Robert Argand described the geometric picture of the complex plane, and Carl Friedrich Gauss made it widely accepted.

## Uses

* **Electrical engineering**: alternating currents and voltages are described with complex numbers; engineers often write $j$ instead of $i$, because $i$ already means current.
* **Signals and waves**: the Fourier transform breaks sounds, images and radio signals into rotating complex waves.
* **Physics**: the Schrödinger equation of [[quantum-mechanics|quantum mechanics]] contains $i$, and quantum states are described by complex numbers.
* **Mathematics**: by the fundamental theorem of algebra, every polynomial equation has a solution among the complex numbers.

Other number systems extend the real numbers in different ways, such as the anticommuting [[grassmann-number|Grassmann numbers]]. See also [[set-mathematics|Set (mathematics)]].

entries.title: Julia (programming language)
entries.summary: Julia is a free, open-source, high-level programming language designed for fast numerical and scientific computing, built around multiple dispatch and just-in-time compilation.
entries.body:
{{unreferenced}}

**Julia** is a free and open-source, high-level programming language designed for **fast numerical and scientific computing**. It aims to be as easy to write as languages like Python, MATLAB or R, while running at speeds close to compiled languages like C and Fortran. This addresses the "two-language problem", where researchers prototype in a slow, friendly language and then rewrite their code in a fast, harder one.

Julia was created by **Jeff Bezanson**, **Stefan Karpinski**, **Viral B. Shah** and **Alan Edelman**, starting in 2009. It was announced publicly in 2012 in a blog post titled "Why We Created Julia", and version **1.0**, which promised a stable language, was released in August 2018. Julia is released under the **MIT License**, and its source files use the `.jl` extension.

!#B#Multiple dispatch# !#R#Just-in-time compiled# !#G#MIT licensed# !#PR#Made for science#

## Design

* **Just-in-time compilation**: Julia compiles each function to fast native machine code (through the LLVM compiler framework) the first time it is called with a given combination of argument types.
* **Multiple dispatch**: a function can have many **methods**, and #PR#Julia picks which one to run from the types of all of its arguments##, not just the first one. This is the central idea of the language.
* **Dynamic typing with type inference**: types do not have to be written, but they can be added to methods and structs for clarity and to choose behavior.
* **Built for maths**: arrays, linear algebra, complex numbers (using `im` for the [[imaginary-number|imaginary unit]]), rational numbers and arbitrary-precision numbers are built in. Arrays are indexed from 1, as in mathematics.
* **Unicode names**: code can use symbols such as `π`, `α` or `∑` directly, so formulas can look like they do on paper.
* **Metaprogramming**: Julia code can be treated as data, and **macros** like `@time` transform code before it runs.
* **Interoperability**: Julia can call C and Fortran libraries directly, and packages connect it to Python, R and other languages.

## Examples

A function that counts the steps of the Collatz sequence:

```
function collatz(n::Integer)
    steps = 0
    while n != 1
        n = iseven(n) ? n ÷ 2 : 3n + 1
        steps += 1
    end
    return steps
end
```

Multiple dispatch, choosing a method by the type of shape:

```
abstract type Shape end
struct Circle <: Shape
    r::Float64
end
struct Square <: Shape
    side::Float64
end

area(c::Circle) = π * c.r^2
area(s::Square) = s.side^2

area(Circle(1.0))  # 3.141592653589793
area(Square(2.0))  # 4.0
```

> [!TIP] `3n` means `3 * n`: Julia allows a number to be written right before a variable, as in mathematical notation.

> [!FACT] Julia's logo shows three colored dots: red, green and purple. ^^PR^Hello, Julia!^^

## Ecosystem

Julia comes with an interactive **REPL** (read–eval–print loop) and a built-in package manager, **Pkg**, which installs packages from a public registry. Well-known packages and tools include:

* **DifferentialEquations.jl** for solving differential equations.
* **JuMP** for mathematical optimization.
* **Flux** for machine learning.
* **Plots.jl** and **Makie** for charts and visualization.
* **Pluto** and **Jupyter** notebooks for interactive work (the "Ju" in Jupyter stands for Julia, alongside Python and R).

## Uses

Julia is used in science and engineering for simulation, data analysis, climate and physics modeling (including [[quantum-mechanics|quantum mechanics]] simulations), finance, and high-performance computing on supercomputers and GPUs.

entries.title: Keydown
entries.summary: Keydown is the formatting language of Radii Office, where short tags typed around text turn it into glossy chips, highlights, headings and more.
entries.body:
**Keydown** is the formatting language of [[radii-office|Radii Office]]. Instead of clicking buttons, you type short **tags** around your text, and the text turns into formatting: #G#glossy chips#, %B%gloss pills%, #%O%gel flags%, @neontube-2@unique styles@, =B=gel orbs=B=, #Y#gel highlights##, **bold**, headings, lists and dozens of interactive "applets". Many of its looks come from the [[frutiger-aero|Frutiger Aero]] style. Every example below is drawn live, right on this page.

## How it works

In Writeout and Bitbook, a tag turns into its formatting the moment you press **Space** after it, and pressing **Enter** at the end of a line formats every tag left on that line. In OpenDB, Phosphor and other apps, tags are drawn whenever the text is shown. Most tags wrap your text in an opening and a closing tag, such as `#R#` and `#`. Typing `\\` at the end of a formatted piece steps back out of it.

Writeout and Bitbook can also **Un-format** a whole page, which turns all of its formatting back into tags so mistakes are easy to spot, and **Re-format** it, which formats everything again and underlines any tag that could not be formatted.

Keydown text is saved in `.kd` files (Writeout documents and OpenDB entries) and `.kn` files (Bitbook notes), and those apps can open each other's files.

## Lines

Start a line with one of these and a space:

* `# Heading` makes a big heading, `## Heading` a smaller one and `### Heading` a third level.
* `#### Heading` makes the extra large **mega header**.
* `* item` makes a bullet point, and `> text` a quote.

## Basics

* `**bold**` gives **bold**, and `*italic*` gives *italic*.
* Backticks around a word show it in a `code` font.
* `&&spark&&` gives &&spark&&.

## Gel highlights

Six of the Annotator's tools, as tags: `#R#text##` is a highlight strip, `#R#text#_` a gel underline, `#R#text#~` a gel strike, `#R#text#=` a glossy Gel Box, `#R#text#]` Corner Brackets and `#R#text#-` a Gel Select. They come in 13 colors:

* `#R#` red: #R#highlight## #R#underline#_ #R#strike#~ #R#box#= #R#brackets#] #R#select#-
* `#O#` orange: #O#highlight## #O#underline#_ #O#strike#~ #O#box#= #O#brackets#] #O#select#-
* `#GL#` gold: #GL#highlight## #GL#underline#_ #GL#strike#~ #GL#box#= #GL#brackets#] #GL#select#-
* `#Y#` yellow: #Y#highlight## #Y#underline#_ #Y#strike#~ #Y#box#= #Y#brackets#] #Y#select#-
* `#L#` lime: #L#highlight## #L#underline#_ #L#strike#~ #L#box#= #L#brackets#] #L#select#-
* `#G#` green: #G#highlight## #G#underline#_ #G#strike#~ #G#box#= #G#brackets#] #G#select#-
* `#TU#` turquoise: #TU#highlight## #TU#underline#_ #TU#strike#~ #TU#box#= #TU#brackets#] #TU#select#-
* `#T#` teal: #T#highlight## #T#underline#_ #T#strike#~ #T#box#= #T#brackets#] #T#select#-
* `#C#` cyan: #C#highlight## #C#underline#_ #C#strike#~ #C#box#= #C#brackets#] #C#select#-
* `#B#` blue: #B#highlight## #B#underline#_ #B#strike#~ #B#box#= #B#brackets#] #B#select#-
* `#PR#` purple: #PR#highlight## #PR#underline#_ #PR#strike#~ #PR#box#= #PR#brackets#] #PR#select#-
* `#PK#` pink: #PK#highlight## #PK#underline#_ #PK#strike#~ #PK#box#= #PK#brackets#] #PK#select#-
* `#SL#` slate: #SL#highlight## #SL#underline#_ #SL#strike#~ #SL#box#= #SL#brackets#] #SL#select#-

## Writing a symbol as itself

To keep a symbol from acting as formatting, put a backslash in front of it. The backslash disappears and the symbol stays as it is:

* `\#R#not a chip#` shows \#R#not a chip#
* `\*\*not bold\*\*` shows \*\*not bold\*\*
* `\^\^B^no speech bubble^^` shows \^\^B^no speech bubble^^
* `\\` shows a single backslash: \\

Only symbols are affected: a backslash before a letter or a number stays, so paths like `C:\Users` are safe.

entries.title: A public-domain knowledge base without a server
entries.summary: How OpenDB stores articles, media and papers as reviewable text files and serves them as a static site with instant client-side search.
entries.abstract: Open knowledge projects usually depend on a database server, which brings hosting costs, operational risk and a single point of failure. We describe OpenDB, a public-domain (CC0) knowledge base that needs none. Each entry is a plain text file with a short header of facts followed by Keydown content with LaTeX math. A build step compiles all entries into one index file that a static website loads once and searches entirely in the browser. Contributions are prepared in the browser, saved locally right away, and submitted as reviewable changes to a public repository, so history, moderation and backups come from version control. We discuss the trade-offs of this design, including slower publication and the size limits of a single index, and why dedicating everything to the public domain simplifies reuse.
entries.body:
## 1. Motivation

Encyclopedias, media archives and preprint servers share a goal: make knowledge easy to find and reuse. Running them usually means operating databases and servers. [[opendb|OpenDB]] explores a smaller design that can be hosted on any static web host.

## 2. Entries as text files

Every entry is a text file. A header lists its id, type (article, media or paper), title, summary, tags, dates, authors and license, followed by Keydown content (the formatting language of Radii Office) with optional LaTeX math. Files are easy to read, review and edit, and every change is recorded by version control.

## 3. One index, searched in the browser

A build script parses every entry, checks required fields, rejects any license other than CC0, and writes a single index file. The site downloads this file once and keeps it in memory. Search scores titles, tags, summaries and full text, so results appear as you type without any server round trip.

## 4. Contributions

The editor shows a live preview and requires the contributor to dedicate the work to the public domain. The entry is saved on the contributor's device immediately and can be submitted as a proposed new file to the public repository. A maintainer reviews it, then rebuilds the index.

## 5. Trade-offs

Publication waits for review instead of being instant, and one index file eventually becomes large. Splitting the index by collection or first letter, and loading full text only on demand, would let the design grow much further.

## 6. Why CC0

Because every entry is dedicated to the [[public-domain|public domain]] under [[cc0|CC0]], reusers never need to track attribution or license versions, which removes the most common barrier to reusing open material.

entries.title: OpenDB
entries.summary: OpenDB is an open-access database of articles, media and papers, all dedicated to the public domain under CC0.
entries.body:
**OpenDB** is a free, open-access database of knowledge. Everything in it, from encyclopedia articles to pictures and research papers, is dedicated to the [[public-domain|public domain]] under [[cc0|CC0]]. That means anyone can copy, change, translate, sell or build on any entry, for any purpose, without asking and without giving credit.[^1]

## Collections

OpenDB has three collections:

* **Articles**: encyclopedia entries that explain a topic, like [[photosynthesis]] or the [[pythagorean-theorem|Pythagorean theorem]].
* **Media**: images, diagrams, sounds and other files that are free to reuse, each with a description.
* **Papers**: research papers and preprints with an abstract, authors and categories, ready to cite.

## How it works

Every entry is a small text file with a few facts at the top (its title, summary, tags and dates) and the content below, written in **Keydown**, the formatting language used across Radii Office. Keydown gives entries headings, lists and glossy styles like =B=gel orbs=B=, #G#bubble chips#, ^^B^speech bubbles^^, #Y#gel highlights## and %16%PK%Gel Sparkles%##, and entries can include LaTeX math such as $e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0$. The files live in a public repository, so every change is recorded and reviewable. When you contribute, OpenDB prepares the file for you and you submit it as a proposal, which a maintainer reviews before it appears for everyone.

Articles can also hold quotes and callout boxes, written as lines that start with `> `:

> [!TIP] Write `> [!NOTE]`, `> [!TIP]`, `> [!IMPORTANT]`, `> [!WARNING]`, `> [!CAUTION]` or `> [!FACT]` to make a box like this one!

Entries link to each other with double square brackets, so writing `[[water-cycle]]` creates a link to the [[water-cycle|water cycle]] article, and each entry shows what links to it.

> [!NOTE] Every change to OpenDB is reviewed by a maintainer before it appears for everyone.

## Why CC0?

Many open projects use licenses that require attribution or require that changes be shared under the same license. Those rules are useful, but they also make reuse harder: a teacher, a game maker or a researcher has to track credits and license versions. CC0 removes those steps. Anything in OpenDB can be used anywhere, in any way, forever.

## References

[^1]: Creative Commons, "CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication", https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/

entries.title: Perma: a small language with permanent, changeable and kept bindings
entries.summary: We describe Perma, a beginner-friendly language whose bindings are permanent (let), changeable (var) or kept across runs (keep), running both on its own and inside web pages.
entries.abstract: Beginner languages usually offer one kind of variable, leaving learners to discover by accident which values are meant to change and which values should survive after a program ends. Perma makes both choices explicit in the syntax. A let binding can never be reassigned, a var binding can, and a keep binding is automatically saved and restored between runs, in a file on the command line and in browser storage on the web. We describe the language, its tree-walking interpreter, the rules that make kept values persist even when they are changed in place, and a runtime that lets Perma run from script tags in ordinary web pages. A test suite of 66 cases covers the language and its command-line tool.
entries.body:
## 1. Introduction

New programmers meet variables early, but most languages treat every variable the same way. Two important questions stay hidden: *is this value supposed to change?* and *should this value still be here next time?* Perma answers both in the syntax with three keywords: `let`, `var` and `keep`.

## 2. Three kinds of bindings

* `let name = value` creates a **permanent** binding. Assigning to it again is an error that explains how to make the value changeable.
* `var name = value` creates a **changeable** binding.
* `keep name = value` creates a **kept** binding. The first run stores the starting value; later runs load the stored value instead.

A permanent binding still refers to the same list or map, but the contents of that list or map can change. This mirrors how many languages treat constants and keeps simple programs such as to-do lists natural to write.

## 3. Keeping changes that happen in place

Saving a kept value on assignment is not enough, because programs often change kept data in place, for example `push(todos, "milk")`. Perma therefore saves every kept binding after each program run and after each event handler or timer callback finishes. Assignments through fields and indexes, such as `todos[0].done = true`, also save the kept value at the root of the expression.

## 4. Running on its own and on the web

The interpreter is a single dependency-free file. On the command line, kept values are stored per program in the user's home folder. In a browser, programs written in `<script type="text/perma">` tags run automatically, share one global environment like ordinary scripts, and store kept values in local storage. A small page interface (`page.find`, `el.on`, `el.text`) lets programs build interfaces without HTML knowledge.

## 5. Friendly failure

Errors name the line and suggest fixes, such as a misspelled name (*did you mean count?*). A step limit stops endless loops, and runaway recursion becomes a readable error instead of a crash.

## 6. Conclusion

Making permanence and persistence visible in the syntax costs only two extra keywords, yet it lets beginners express intent and build small useful programs, like counters and to-do lists that remember their data, in a few lines.

entries.title: Photosynthesis
entries.summary: Photosynthesis is the process plants, algae and some bacteria use to turn light, water and carbon dioxide into sugar and oxygen.
entries.body:
{{unreferenced}}

**Photosynthesis** is the process by which plants, algae and some bacteria capture the energy of light and store it in sugar. It produces the oxygen in Earth's air and is #G#the starting point of almost every food chain##.

## The overall reaction

In plants, photosynthesis can be summarized as:

$$6\,\mathrm{CO_2} + 6\,\mathrm{H_2O} \xrightarrow{\text{light}} \mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6} + 6\,\mathrm{O_2}$$

Six molecules of carbon dioxide and six of water become one molecule of glucose and six molecules of oxygen.

::gemerald{In short|Light + water + carbon dioxide make sugar + oxygen}

![What goes into a leaf, and what comes out](media:photosynthesis-diagram)

## Where it happens

In plants and algae, photosynthesis takes place in **chloroplasts**, small structures inside cells. Chloroplasts contain #G#chlorophyll#, a green pigment that absorbs red and blue light strongly and reflects green light, which is why leaves look green.

## Two stages

#^Y^Stage 1: light^ #^G^Stage 2: Calvin cycle^

1. **Light-dependent reactions**: in the thylakoid membranes, light energy splits water molecules. This releases oxygen and produces energy carriers called ATP and NADPH.
2. **The Calvin cycle**: in the stroma around the thylakoids, the cell uses ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide from the air into sugars.

## Importance

> [!FACT] Almost all of the oxygen in the air you breathe was released by photosynthesis.

Photosynthesis provides the oxygen that most living things breathe and the energy stored in food. Fossil fuels such as coal and oil are made from the remains of organisms that once captured energy this way. The water a plant takes in is part of the [[water-cycle|water cycle]], and some of it returns to the air through transpiration.

entries.title: Prime number
entries.summary: A prime number is a whole number greater than 1 whose only divisors are 1 and itself.
entries.body:
{{unreferenced}}

A **prime number** is a whole number greater than 1 that can only be divided evenly by 1 and by itself. Numbers greater than 1 that are not prime are called **composite**.

## Examples

The first prime numbers are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23 and 29:

%1%R%2%## %1%O%3%## %1%GL%5%## %1%Y%7%## %1%L%11%## %1%G%13%## %1%TU%17%## %1%C%19%## %1%B%23%## %1%PR%29%##

The number 2 is the only even prime, because every other even number can be divided by 2.

> [!IMPORTANT] The number 1 is not prime: a prime has exactly two different divisors, 1 and itself, and 1 has only one.

## Building blocks of numbers

The **fundamental theorem of arithmetic** says #Y#every whole number greater than 1 can be written as a product of primes in exactly one way## (apart from the order). For example, $60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5$.

## Infinitely many primes

Around 300 BC, the Greek mathematician Euclid proved that the primes never run out. If there were only finitely many, $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$, you could multiply them all together and add 1 to get $N = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_n + 1$. The result would leave remainder 1 when divided by every prime on the list, so it would need a prime factor that was missing from the list.

> [!FACT] The largest known primes are **Mersenne primes**, numbers of the form $2^p - 1$.

## Finding primes

A simple way to list primes is the **sieve of Eratosthenes**: write the numbers from 2 upward, then repeatedly circle the next uncrossed number and cross out all of its multiples. The circled numbers are the primes.

![The sieve of Eratosthenes for the numbers 1 to 50](media:sieve-of-eratosthenes)

Primes are used in modern cryptography, because multiplying two large primes is easy while recovering them from the product is extremely hard. See also the [[pythagorean-theorem|Pythagorean theorem]].

entries.title: Public domain
entries.summary: The public domain is the body of creative work that no one owns, so anyone may use it freely.
entries.body:
{{unreferenced}}

The **public domain** is made up of creative works that are not protected by copyright or similar exclusive rights. Because no one owns them, #G#anyone may copy, adapt, perform, publish or sell them## without permission.

## How works enter the public domain

A work can enter the public domain in several ways:

#%SL%Expiration% #%Y%Ineligibility% #%G%Dedication% #%B%Government works%

1. **Expiration**: copyright lasts for a limited time. In many countries it ends a set number of years after the author's death, often 70 years.
2. **Ineligibility**: some things cannot be copyrighted at all, such as plain facts, ideas, and in many places short phrases or works with no creative choices.
3. **Dedication**: an author can give up their rights on purpose, for example with the [[cc0|CC0]] public domain dedication.
4. **Government works**: in some countries, works made by the national government are not copyrighted. In the United States this applies to works made by federal employees as part of their jobs.

## Why it matters

The public domain is a shared foundation for culture and science. Classic novels, old paintings and music, mathematical results and historical records can be republished, remixed and taught without cost. Projects like [[opendb|OpenDB]] add to it by publishing new work directly into the public domain.

> [!TIP] Everything in [[opendb|OpenDB]] is in the public domain from the day it is published, through [[cc0|CC0]].

entries.title: Pythagorean theorem
entries.summary: In a right triangle, the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides.
entries.body:
{{unreferenced}}

The **Pythagorean theorem** is a basic fact of geometry about right triangles, the triangles with one 90° angle. It says that the area of the square on the longest side (the **hypotenuse**) equals the total area of the squares on the other two sides.

![Squares on the sides of a 3-4-5 triangle](media:pythagoras-diagram)

## Statement

If the two shorter sides have lengths *a* and *b*, and the hypotenuse has length *c*, then:

$$a^2 + b^2 = c^2$$

::gsky{Remember it|The two short sides, squared and added, equal the long side squared}

For example, a triangle with sides 3 and 4 has a hypotenuse of 5, because $3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5^2$.

## Pythagorean triples

Sets of three whole numbers that fit the theorem are called **Pythagorean triples**. Examples include (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13) and (8, 15, 17):

#:R:3, 4, 5: #:O:5, 12, 13: #:Y:8, 15, 17: #:L:6, 8, 10:

 Multiplying a triple by any whole number gives another one, such as (6, 8, 10).

## History and proofs

The theorem is named after the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, but the relationship was known much earlier: a Babylonian clay tablet known as Plimpton 322 lists Pythagorean triples. 

> [!FACT] Plimpton 322 is nearly 4,000 years old: it was made more than a thousand years before Pythagoras was born.

Hundreds of different proofs exist, including proofs that rearrange four copies of the triangle inside a large square.

## Uses

The theorem gives the straight-line distance between two points, so it is used in maps, navigation, construction, computer graphics and physics. It also connects to other number facts, such as which numbers are [[prime-number|prime]] (every prime that leaves remainder 1 when divided by 4 is a sum of two squares).

entries.title: Quantum mechanics
entries.summary: Quantum mechanics is the branch of physics that describes how matter and light behave at the scale of atoms and smaller, where energy comes in discrete amounts and outcomes are described by probabilities.
entries.body:
{{unreferenced}}

**Quantum mechanics** is the branch of physics that describes the behavior of matter and light at the scale of atoms and subatomic particles. At that scale, nature works very differently from everyday experience: energy often comes in fixed packets called **quanta**, particles behave like waves, and the result of a measurement can usually only be predicted as a **probability**.

> I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics.
> — Richard Feynman, *The Character of Physical Law* (1965)

Quantum mechanics is #B#one of the most precisely tested theories in science##. It explains the structure of atoms, chemical bonding, and how light and matter interact, and it underlies technologies such as transistors, lasers and LEDs.

## Key ideas

!#B#Quanta# !#PR#Waves and particles# !#G#Superposition# !#O#Uncertainty# !#PK#Spin# !#TU#Entanglement#

* **Quantization**: some quantities, like the energy of an electron in an atom, can only take certain separate values. In a hydrogen atom the allowed energies are about $E_n = -\dfrac{13.6\ \text{eV}}{n^2}$ for $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$
* **Wave–particle duality**: light and matter show both wave-like behavior (such as interference) and particle-like behavior (such as arriving in single lumps).
* **Superposition**: a system can be in a combination of several states at once, until it is measured.
* **The uncertainty principle**: some pairs of quantities cannot both be known exactly. For position $x$ and momentum $p$, $\Delta x\,\Delta p \ge \dfrac{\hbar}{2}$.
* **Spin**: particles carry an intrinsic angular momentum that comes in fixed amounts; the spins of atomic nuclei are what MRI scanners detect inside a [[solenoid|solenoid]] magnet.
* **Entanglement**: two particles can share one joint state, so that measuring one gives information about the other, however far apart they are.

## The wave function

The state of a quantum system is described by a **wave function**, usually written $\psi$. Its values are complex numbers, built from real and [[imaginary-number|imaginary numbers]]. The wave function changes over time according to the **Schrödinger equation**:

$$i\hbar \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial t} = \hat{H}\psi$$

Here $\hbar$ is the reduced Planck constant ($h / 2\pi$) and $\hat{H}$, the **Hamiltonian**, describes the system's total energy.

> [!IMPORTANT] The wave function itself cannot be observed directly: only the probabilities it gives can be measured.

By the **Born rule**, the probability of finding a particle at a place is proportional to $|\psi|^2$, the squared size of the wave function there.

## History

* **1900**: Max Planck explained the light given off by hot objects by assuming energy is emitted in packets, $E = hf$.
* **1905**: Albert Einstein explained the photoelectric effect by treating light itself as made of quanta, later called photons.
* **1913**: Niels Bohr proposed a model of the hydrogen atom with fixed electron orbits.
* **1924**: Louis de Broglie suggested that particles such as electrons also behave as waves.
* **1925–1926**: Werner Heisenberg developed matrix mechanics, Erwin Schrödinger his wave equation, and Max Born the probability interpretation. Wolfgang Pauli stated the exclusion principle.
* **1927–1930s**: Paul Dirac and others joined quantum mechanics with special relativity, leading toward quantum field theory.

## Interpretations

The mathematics of quantum mechanics is agreed upon, but what it *means* is still debated. The **Copenhagen interpretation** treats the wave function as a tool for predicting measurements; the **many-worlds interpretation** says every possible outcome happens in a branching universe; and other views, such as pilot-wave theory, add hidden details. All of them make the same predictions for ordinary experiments.

## Uses

* **Electronics**: transistors, computer chips, solar cells and LEDs depend on the quantum behavior of electrons in solids.
* **Lasers** rely on stimulated emission of light from atoms.
* **Medicine**: MRI scanners use the quantum property of nuclear spin.
* **Quantum computing** uses superposition and entanglement to process information in new ways.
* **Particle physics**: quantum field theory describes the fundamental particles; fermions such as electrons are handled mathematically with [[grassmann-number|Grassmann numbers]].

entries.title: Radii Office
entries.summary: Radii Office is a free, open-source suite of web apps for documents, spreadsheets, slides, notes, files and more, styled after the Frutiger Aero look.
entries.body:
**Radii Office** is a free suite of web apps for writing, calculating, presenting, taking notes, building websites and handling files. Every app runs right in the web browser, with nothing to install, and keeps your work in the browser on your own device. The apps share a glossy look inspired by [[frutiger-aero|Frutiger Aero]] and a formatting language called [[keydown|Keydown]].

> [!TIP] Every app keeps your work in your own browser, so it stays on your device unless you choose to share it.

## Shared features

* **Two layouts**: each app can switch between an Office-style **ribbon** layout and its original **Classic** layout, with glass sidebars and gel buttons.
* **Keydown**: the same short tags, like #G#chips#, #Y#highlights##, ^^B^speech bubbles^^ and %1%PR%Gel Bevels%##, format text across the apps.
* **Share & Chat**: many apps let people edit the same file together in real time, with chat.
* **Open source**: the code is published on GitHub, and the suite is licensed under CC0 and the MIT License or the Unlicense.

## Writeout

#B#Documents#

**Writeout** is a rich-text writing tool for focused document writing. Its ribbon layout works like Microsoft Word, with a Navigation pane, real pages and a status bar. It supports Keydown, an Annotator for highlighting, equations, footnotes and several pages in one document. Documents are saved as `.kd` files and can be exported as PDF, Word (`.docx`), OpenDocument (`.odt`), plain text and EPUB. Writeout also has a downloadable desktop app.

## Imbuer

#G#Spreadsheet#

**Imbuer** is a spreadsheet: a grid calculator for mathematical analysis, cell formatting and quick data layouts. Its Excel-style ribbon includes formulas, charts and number formats, and its cells understand Keydown text styles. Sheets can be imported and exported as CSV.

## Amber

#GL#Presentation#

**Amber** is a slide presentation studio with glossy 3D shapes, spring-animated menus and a fullscreen presentation mode. Its ribbon layout works like PowerPoint, with Transitions, Animations, a Notes pane and a Slide Sorter. Presentations are saved as `.ka` files.

## Cabinet

#R#Drive#

**Cabinet** is a drive app for keeping files organized in drawers, in a layout like a file explorer. It is designed to be easy to use and quick, and it can download a whole drive at once as a ZIP file. Drives are saved as `.kc` files.

## Mainkey

#PR#Database#

**Mainkey** is a database for keeping records. You build your own fields, then search, filter and sort the records in a table or browse them in a gallery view, with live statistics. A database can even be hosted straight from your browser tab and shared. Databases are saved as `.kb` files and can be imported or exported as CSV.

## Omicron

#TU#Web Builder#

**Omicron** is a visual builder for laying out web pages, crafting templates and creating HTML. Its ribbon layout works like Microsoft Sway, with cards, styles, tags and skills. A page can be exported as a website ZIP or as a single HTML file with every style built in, and Bitbook notes can be inserted into it.

## Inkpath

#PK#Vector Studio#

**Inkpath** is a vector graphics editor. It has box selection for picking several shapes at once, real-time dragging of Bézier curve points, and panning and zooming around the canvas. Its curve math runs in WebAssembly built from Rust. Drawings are saved as `.kv` files and can be exported as SVG.

## Peeker

#O#PDF#

**Peeker** is a PDF editor that runs entirely in the browser, so files are never uploaded anywhere. You can add text, highlights, drawings, boxes, whiteout, pictures and signatures; rotate, reorder, duplicate and delete pages; merge PDFs; fill in forms; and search the text. It uses the open-source pdf.js and pdf-lib libraries.

## Other apps

The suite also includes **Bitbook** for notes, **Waterflow** for fun notes, **Formly** for forms, **Hexa** for calendars and boards, **Taskra** for to-do lists, **Phosphor** for team messaging and [[opendb|OpenDB]], the free database this article is part of.

entries.title: Set (mathematics)
entries.summary: A set is a collection of distinct objects, called its elements, considered as a single object.
entries.body:
{{unreferenced}}

A **set** is a collection of distinct objects, called its **elements** or **members**. A set is defined only by what it contains: #Y#the order of the elements does not matter, and listing an element twice does not change the set##. Sets are one of the most basic ideas in mathematics, and almost every other mathematical object can be built from them.

![Two overlapping sets, A and B, inside a universal set U](media:venn-diagram)

## Writing sets

A small set can be written by listing its elements between curly braces, such as $A = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$. Because order and repetition do not matter, $\{1, 2, 3\}$, $\{3, 1, 2\}$ and $\{1, 1, 2, 3\}$ are all the same set.

Larger sets are often described by a rule instead, using **set-builder notation**: $\{x \mid x \text{ is an even number}\}$ is read "the set of all $x$ such that $x$ is even".

* $x \in A$ means "$x$ is an element of $A$", and $x \notin A$ means it is not.
* The **empty set**, written $\varnothing$ or $\{\}$, has no elements at all.
* The **cardinality** of a finite set, written $|A|$, is how many elements it has. For example, $|\{1, 2, 3, 4\}| = 4$.

## Subsets

A set $A$ is a **subset** of $B$, written $A \subseteq B$, when every element of $A$ is also in $B$. Every set is a subset of itself, and the empty set is a subset of every set. The **power set** of $A$ is the set of all of its subsets; a set with $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets.

## Operations

For the sets $A = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ and $B = \{3, 4, 5, 6\}$ shown in the diagram:

* **Union**: $A \cup B = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$, everything in $A$, in $B$, or in both.
* **Intersection**: $A \cap B = \{3, 4\}$, only what both sets share.
* **Difference**: $A \setminus B = \{1, 2\}$, what is in $A$ but not in $B$.
* **Complement**: everything in the universal set $U$ that is not in $A$.

> [!TIP] An easy way to remember: union is like "or", and intersection is like "and".

Two sets with no elements in common, so that $A \cap B = \varnothing$, are called **disjoint**. Drawings like the one above are called **Venn diagrams**.

## Common number sets

^^B^ℕ natural^^ ^^G^ℤ integers^^ ^^PR^ℚ rational^^ ^^O^ℝ real^^

Some sets are used so often that they have their own symbols: $\mathbb{N}$ for the natural numbers, $\mathbb{Z}$ for the integers, $\mathbb{Q}$ for the rational numbers and $\mathbb{R}$ for the real numbers. The [[prime-number|prime numbers]] also form a set, and it is infinite.

entries.title: Solar System
entries.summary: The Solar System is the Sun and everything that orbits it, including eight planets and their moons.
entries.body:
{{unreferenced}}

The **Solar System** is made up of the Sun and everything bound to it by gravity: eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids, comets and dust. It formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust.

![The planets in order (not to scale)](media:solar-system-diagram)

## The planets

In order from the Sun, the planets are:

1. #SL#Mercury#: the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun.
2. #Y#Venus#: the hottest planet, wrapped in thick clouds.
3. #B#Earth#: the only planet known to have life.
4. #R#Mars#: a cold, red, rocky planet.
5. #O#Jupiter#: the largest planet, a gas giant.
6. #GL#Saturn#: a gas giant famous for its bright rings.
7. #C#Uranus#: an ice giant that spins tipped on its side.
8. #PR#Neptune#: the windiest and most distant planet.

The first four are small and rocky; the outer four are giants. Between Mars and Jupiter lies the **asteroid belt**, and beyond Neptune is the **Kuiper belt**, home to Pluto and many icy bodies.

> [!FACT] Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to travel from the Sun to Earth.

## The Sun

The Sun holds #GL#more than 99.8% of the Solar System's mass##. Its light powers Earth's weather, the [[water-cycle|water cycle]] and [[photosynthesis]].

entries.title: Solenoid
entries.summary: A solenoid is a coil of wire wound into a tight helix, which makes a strong, nearly uniform magnetic field inside it when an electric current flows through it.
entries.body:
{{images needed|a photo of a solenoid}}
{{unreferenced}}

A **solenoid** is a long coil of wire wound into a tightly packed helix. When an electric current flows through the wire, the coil produces a magnetic field. Inside a long solenoid this field is strong and nearly **uniform**, pointing along the coil's axis, while outside it is much weaker. This makes solenoids one of the simplest ways to make a controlled magnetic field, and the basic part inside many electromagnets.

The name comes from the Greek *sōlēn*, meaning "pipe" or "channel", and was introduced by the French physicist André-Marie Ampère in the 1820s.

## The magnetic field

For an ideal solenoid (very long, with closely spaced turns and nothing but air inside), the field inside is

$$B = \mu_0 n I$$

::gsky{Field inside an ideal solenoid|B = μ₀ n I: more turns per meter or more current means a stronger field}

where $\mu_0$ is the magnetic constant (the permeability of free space), $n$ is the number of turns per unit length and $I$ is the current. #B#The field does not depend on the coil's width or on where you are inside it##, which is why it is so uniform. The result follows from **Ampère's law** applied to a rectangular loop that passes through the inside of the coil.

The direction of the field follows the **right-hand rule**: if the fingers of your right hand curl the way the current flows around the coil, your thumb points the way the field points inside it, toward the coil's north end.

* More turns per meter, or more current, makes a stronger field.
* Filling the coil with a **ferromagnetic core**, such as soft iron, multiplies the field by the core's relative permeability $\mu_r$, which can be hundreds or thousands of times stronger, until the core saturates.
* A real solenoid of finite length has a weaker, spreading field near its ends.

## Inductance

Because a solenoid stores energy in its magnetic field, it resists changes in current. Its **inductance** is about

$$L = \frac{\mu_0 N^2 A}{\ell}$$

for $N$ turns, cross-sectional area $A$ and length $\ell$. This makes solenoids useful as **inductors** in electrical circuits, and explains the spark that can jump when a coil's current is switched off suddenly.

> [!WARNING] Switching off a coil suddenly can make a high-voltage spike, so circuits that drive solenoids usually add a protective diode.

## Uses

* **Solenoid actuators**: a movable iron plunger is pulled into the coil when it is switched on, turning electricity into a short, straight push or pull. These drive door locks, pinball flippers and many machines.
* **Solenoid valves** open and close the flow of water, gas or fuel, for example in washing machines and irrigation systems.
* **Relays** and car **starter solenoids** use a small current to switch a much larger one.
* **MRI scanners** use large superconducting solenoids to make the very strong, very uniform field needed for medical imaging (see [[quantum-mechanics|quantum mechanics]] for the spin physics behind it).
* Loudspeakers, electric bells and many sensors also rely on coils.

## Not to be confused with

In mathematics, a **solenoid** is also the name of a kind of topological space built from nested, wrapped-around loops. It shares only the name with the electromagnetic coil.

entries.title: Water cycle
entries.summary: The water cycle is the continuous movement of water between the oceans, the air and the land.
entries.body:
{{unreferenced}}

The **water cycle**, or hydrologic cycle, describes how water moves around Earth. #C#The total amount of water stays almost the same##, but it constantly changes between liquid, vapor and ice as it travels between the oceans, the atmosphere and the land.

![The water cycle](media:water-cycle-diagram)

## Main stages

* #^O^Evaporation^: the Sun heats water in oceans, lakes and rivers, turning some of it into water vapor.
* #^G^Transpiration^: plants release water vapor through tiny pores in their leaves. Together with evaporation this is called evapotranspiration.
* #^SL^Condensation^: as moist air rises it cools, and the vapor condenses into tiny droplets that form clouds.
* #^B^Precipitation^: droplets join into larger drops and fall as rain, snow, sleet or hail.
* #^TU^Runoff and infiltration^: water flows over the ground into streams and back to the sea, or soaks into the soil to become groundwater.

> [!FACT] The water in your glass has been evaporated, rained down and carried to the sea countless times.

## Why it matters

The water cycle delivers fresh water to land, shapes weather and climate, and carries heat around the planet. Plants depend on it for the water they use in [[photosynthesis]].
